rawText: When a short link has expired and returns an expiry error response instead of redirecting, the resolution attempt is still recorded as a click in analytics. Click counts must only be incremented when a redirect actually occurs (i.e., the visitor is successfully sent to the destination URL).
normalizedProblem: When a short link has expired and returns an expiry error response instead of redirecting, the resolution attempt is still recorded as a click in analytics. Click counts must only be incremented when a redirect actually occurs (i.e., the visitor is successfully sent to the destination URL).

acceptanceCriteria.description: When a short link is expired and a resolution attempt is made, the click count for that link MUST NOT increase.

When a short link is expired and a resolution attempt is made, any other analytics event (e.g., a raw-hit or failed-resolution event, if such exist) MUST NOT be counted as or converted into a click event.
When a short link is valid and a successful redirect (HTTP 3xx) is issued, the click count MUST continue to be incremented exactly as before.

Historical click counts that were inflated by expired-link resolution attempts are acknowledged as already incorrect; this fix applies only to events recorded after the fix is deployed (no retroactive correction is specified by this requirement).

The expiry check and the click-recording step must be logically coupled so that a click is recorded if and only if the expiry check passes and a redirect response is produced, with no race condition window in which the check passes but expiry occurs before the count is written.
The expired-link response returned to the visitor (e.g., HTTP 410 Gone or equivalent) is unaffected by this fix and must remain correct.

ambiguities: The requirement says 'not counted as a click since the visitor was not actually sent anywhere.' It is unclear whether a resolution attempt on an expired link should be recorded at all (e.g., as a distinct 'attempted-after-expiry' event for audit purposes), or completely discarded from all analytics.

The requirement does not define what 'click' means in the data model — whether it is a single counter, a time-series record, a raw event log, or all of the above. The fix scope depends on which of these must be corrected.

It is not specified whether the same no-count rule applies to other non-redirect outcomes, such as links that are disabled, deleted, or over their usage-cap limit — or whether this fix is strictly scoped to expiry-based failures only.
The exact HTTP status code returned for expired links is not stated, which may affect how the fix is implemented if click recording is currently triggered by inspecting the response code.
assumptions: Assumption (for confirmation): Resolution attempts on expired links should be completely excluded from click analytics and not recorded under any alternative event category, unless a separate 'failed resolution' analytics feature is explicitly designed.

Assumption (for confirmation): The fix is scoped only to expiry-based non-redirects; other non-redirect conditions (disabled links, missing links, quota-exceeded links) are out of scope for this bug report and would require separate tickets.
Assumption (for confirmation): No retroactive correction of already-inflated historical click counts is required as part of this fix.
Assumption (for confirmation): The expiry check is authoritative on the server side; client-supplied timestamps or cache layers do not bypass the server-side check.
outOfScope: Retroactive correction or backfilling of click counts that were incorrectly recorded before this fix is deployed.
Changes to the expiry response returned to the end-user (status code, body, headers).
Analytics behavior for non-expiry failure modes (404 not found, disabled links, rate-limited links) unless explicitly linked to this ticket.
Frontend or dashboard display changes beyond what naturally follows from the corrected underlying count data.
